For decades, Africa was primarily viewed through the lens of development assistance, commodity exports and demographic potential. Today, a different narrative is emerging. Across global boardrooms, sovereign wealth funds and government ministries, Africa is increasingly being discussed not as a future opportunity, but as a strategic necessity. The shift is being driven by a convergence of forces. The global energy transition requires critical minerals. Artificial intelligence requires data centres and power. Supply chains require new logistics corridors. Food security requires agricultural investment. In each of these areas, Africa occupies a position of growing importance. The continent holds some of the world’s largest reserves of cobalt, copper, graphite, manganese, lithium and rare earth minerals. These resources are essential for electric vehicles, batteries, renewable energy systems and advanced technologies. As countries seek to reduce dependence on concentrated supply chains, Africa’s role in the global minerals economy is becoming increasingly strategic. At the same time, Africa’s energy landscape is attracting unprecedented attention. From natural gas developments in Mozambique, Senegal and Mauritania to large-scale renewable energy projects in South Africa, Egypt, Morocco and Kenya, the continent is emerging as a critical component of global energy security. The energy transition is no longer simply a climate story in Africa; it is increasingly an industrialisation and investment story. Infrastructure is playing an equally important role. Strategic projects such as the Lobito Corridor, linking Angola’s Atlantic coast to the mineral-rich regions of Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo, are reshaping trade routes and investment priorities. Across the continent, new ports, railways, transmission lines and industrial zones are being developed to connect production centres with international markets. The digital economy is creating another layer of strategic relevance. As demand for cloud computing, artificial intelligence and digital services accelerates, investment in data centres, fibre networks and digital infrastructure is expanding rapidly. Cities such as Nairobi, Lagos, Johannesburg, Kigali and Cairo are positioning themselves as technology and innovation hubs capable of serving regional and international markets. This growing strategic importance is attracting a wider range of investors than ever before. Gulf sovereign wealth funds are expanding their footprint in African infrastructure and logistics. Western governments are supporting strategic transport and mineral corridors. Asian investors continue to play a major role in manufacturing, mining and industrial development. Increasingly, Africa is becoming a meeting point for competing commercial and geopolitical interests. Yet the most important story may not be external interest. It is the growing determination of African governments and businesses to capture more value from their resources and markets. Across sectors, policymakers are pursuing industrialisation strategies, promoting local processing and encouraging investment in value-added industries. The objective is clear: move beyond exporting raw materials and build stronger domestic economic ecosystems. The result is a continent that is becoming increasingly central to discussions about energy security, supply chains, food production, digital infrastructure and industrial growth. Africa is no longer simply a participant in global economic trends. It is becoming one of the forces shaping them. The rise of Strategic Africa reflects a broader reality. The continent’s future significance will not be defined solely by its population growth or natural resources, but by its ability to position itself at the centre of the industries, technologies and trade routes that will define the global economy in the decades ahead. From power grids and data centres to logistics corridors and industrial hubs, Africa is laying the foundations for a new era of economic growth. For decades, the African growth narrative was dominated by commodities, demographics and development assistance. Today, a different story is beginning to emerge across the continent. From renewable energy projects and digital infrastructure to transport corridors and industrial ecosystems, Africa is increasingly investing in the physical and digital foundations that underpin long-term economic transformation. The shift is visible across multiple sectors. Renewable energy deployment is accelerating, data centres are expanding into new markets, strategic transport corridors are connecting resource-rich regions to global markets, and governments are placing greater emphasis on industrialisation and value addition rather than raw commodity exports. Individually, these projects may appear disconnected. Collectively, they point to something larger: the early stages of what could become Africa’s infrastructure decade. Energy Moves From Constraint to Opportunity Energy has historically been one of Africa’s biggest barriers to growth. Today, it is becoming one of its largest investment opportunities. Solar, wind, battery storage and transmission projects are attracting growing levels of public and private capital. Countries such as South Africa, Egypt, Morocco, Kenya and Ethiopia are expanding generation capacity while investing in the grid infrastructure needed to support industrial growth. At the same time, natural gas continues to play a strategic role in markets such as Mozambique, Tanzania, Senegal, Mauritania and Nigeria, providing baseload power and supporting industrial development. The conversation is gradually shifting from energy scarcity to energy competitiveness. Logistics Corridors Are Redrawing Economic Maps Across Africa, strategic infrastructure corridors are creating new trade routes and investment opportunities. The Lobito Corridor linking Angola to Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo is emerging as one of the continent’s most important logistics projects. Similar investments in ports, railways and highways are reducing transport bottlenecks and improving access to regional and international markets. These corridors are not simply transport projects. They are economic platforms capable of supporting mining, agriculture, manufacturing and regional trade. As implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area continues, the importance of logistics infrastructure will only increase. The Digital Infrastructure Race Accelerates Africa’s digital economy increasingly depends on infrastructure rather than applications alone. Data centres, fibre networks, cloud computing facilities, digital identity systems and payment platforms are becoming critical economic assets. Governments and private investors alike are recognising that digital competitiveness requires substantial physical investment. The emergence of AI and advanced computing is further increasing demand for electricity, connectivity and data-processing capacity. Cities such as Nairobi, Lagos, Johannesburg, Kigali and Cairo are positioning themselves as regional technology hubs, supported by growing digital infrastructure ecosystems. Industrialisation Returns to the Agenda Infrastructure investment is increasingly linked to industrial policy. Nigeria’s Dangote Refinery demonstrates how large-scale industrial projects can reshape value chains by moving countries further up the production ladder. Across the continent, governments are pursuing policies designed to encourage local processing, manufacturing and value addition. The objective is clear: export fewer raw materials and capture more economic value domestically. This strategy is particularly visible in sectors such as critical minerals, agriculture, energy and manufacturing. A New Investment Narrative Perhaps the most significant change is how investors increasingly view Africa. The continent is no longer being seen solely as a source of raw materials or a frontier consumer market. Instead, it is increasingly viewed as a strategic infrastructure market where long-term investments can support decades of economic expansion. This trend is attracting capital from development finance institutions, sovereign wealth funds, pension funds, private equity firms and strategic corporate investors. While challenges remain, including financing gaps, regulatory uncertainty and infrastructure deficits, the direction of travel is becoming increasingly clear. The Foundations Are Being Built Africa’s future growth will not be determined solely by commodity prices or population growth. It will increasingly depend on the infrastructure that connects markets, powers industries, moves goods, stores data and enables innovation. The projects making headlines today may ultimately be remembered as the foundations of a much larger transformation. The story emerging across the continent is not simply one of growth. It is one of construction. Africa’s infrastructure decade may already have begun. The post Africa’s Infrastructure Decade Has Arrived appeared first on FurtherAfrica.

title: Dangote Refinery Expansion is Reshaping Nigeria’s Role in Global Fuel Markets
summary:
Dangote refinery expansion eyes 1.4m bpd capacity and a merchant model that could make Lagos a global fuel hub.

The post Dangote Refinery Expansion is Reshaping Nigeria’s Role in Global Fuel Markets appeared first on FurtherAfrica.
full_text: Dangote Refinery Expansion is Reshaping Nigeria’s Role in Global Fuel Markets Dangote refinery expansion eyes 1.4m bpd capacity and a merchant model that could make Lagos a global fuel hub. The post Dangote Refinery Expansion is Reshaping Nigeria’s Role in Global Fuel Markets appeared first on FurtherAfrica. The Dangote refinery expansion is moving Nigeria from crude exporter to potential global fuel hub.   Dangote’s Lagos refinery is moving beyond its original role as a domestic fuel solution. The expansion now targets a fully merchant model that could pull Nigeria up the value chain. From national refinery to merchant mega-hub The Dangote Petroleum Refinery has a nameplate capacity of 650,000 barrels per day, making it Africa’s largest refinery, and is in the process of ramping up operations toward that level. This confirms its status as Africa’s largest refinery. At this scale, it already reshapes Nigeria’s fuel balance and cuts dependence on imported petrol and diesel. Management is now signalling a much larger ambition. According to Dangote Refinery’s management, the complex is being designed to process a wide range of crude grades well beyond Nigeria’s domestic blends, with plans to significantly expand its crude slate diversity over time. That shift turns a large refinery into a trading asset. It allows operators to switch feedstock rapidly as arbitrage opens and closes across regions. The refinery is processing Nigerian crude and is being configured to handle a variety of international crude grades as its operations ramp up. It is preparing to take heavier grades and supplies from the Middle East and other producing regions. This approach mirrors Singapore and other global hubs. Those hubs rely on diversified crude intake, blending and large storage to maximise margins through the cycle. There has been public discussion about potential future expansions of the refinery complex beyond its current 650,000 barrels per day design capacity, but no formally announced, detailed plan to increase capacity to around 1.4 million barrels per day has been confirmed by major public sources. At that level, the Lagos complex would sit in the top tier of global refining centres by size. It would rank alongside the largest Asian and Middle Eastern facilities. It would require sustained access to international crude markets. It would become a price-sensitive buyer of seaborne barrels, not only a domestic off-taker of Nigerian crude. Singapore-style energy ecosystem in Lagos Management describes the refinery as a fully merchant refining model rather than a plant tied to a single pipeline and crude stream. The strategy relies on building an integrated energy ecosystem on the Lekki site. Alongside refining, Dangote is developing storage facilities, petrochemical production, logistics networks, export infrastructure and crude-blending capabilities. Together, these assets support a crude trading and fuel-export platform rather than a stand-alone refinery. The benefits are already visible in product markets. As regional product markets tightened, Dangote increased its output and export of aviation fuel, taking advantage of favorable margins and demand conditions. According to shipping and trade flow data providers, Dangote has rapidly emerged as a significant exporter of jet fuel from West Africa, but there is no evidence that it has become the world’s largest jet fuel exporter. The pivot showed how quickly the plant can respond to global demand. It also showed how its merchant model can monetise dislocations in trade flows. The refinery is expected to produce significant volumes of petrol as it ramps up, using a range of feedstocks and blending components, in addition to its production of diesel, jet fuel and naphtha. This further increases operational flexibility and supports higher throughput even when local crude supply or specifications constrain output. For Africa, the implications are material. Many countries still rely on imported refined products from Europe, Asia and the Middle East. As Dangote’s export capability grows, West, Central and parts of Southern Africa could see a gradual shift in supply routes towards Lagos. That would shorten voyages, reduce exposure to distant supply shocks and, over time, influence regional fuel pricing benchmarks. For investors, the Dangote refinery expansion points to a structural re-rating of Nigeria’s role in global energy flows. The project deepens demand for midstream infrastructure, storage and marine services along the Gulf of Guinea. It also raises the strategic value of Nigerian ports, pipelines and petrochemical feedstock chains tied into the Lekki complex. The next phase to watch is how quickly Dangote secures crude diversity at scale and locks in logistics to support sustained exports across Africa and beyond. title: Nigeria’s New MVNO Rules Aim to Unlock Competition and Investment
summary:
Nigeria MVNO rules tighten onboarding timelines and commercial oversight — what it means for digital infrastructure investors.

The post Nigeria’s New MVNO Rules Aim to Unlock Competition and Investment appeared first on FurtherAfrica.
full_text: Nigeria’s New MVNO Rules Aim to Unlock Competition and Investment Nigeria MVNO rules tighten onboarding timelines and commercial oversight — what it means for digital infrastructure investors. The post Nigeria’s New MVNO Rules Aim to Unlock Competition and Investment appeared first on FurtherAfrica. Nigeria MVNO rules are being overhauled as the country’s telecoms regulator issues draft Business Rules designed to end onboarding delays and opaque commercial practices that have held back the sector.   Nigeria’s telecoms regulator has moved to reset the rules of engagement between mobile virtual network operators and host operators, issuing draft Business Rules that directly target the onboarding delays and opaque commercial practices that have held back the sector. The new rules aim to impose tighter timelines, clearer allocation of responsibilities and direct regulatory oversight of key agreements, in a bid to unlock a market with clear upside for digital infrastructure and consumer connectivity investors. Tighter onboarding timelines and mandatory transparency The Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) has published Draft Business Rules for Mobile Virtual Network Operators in Nigeria, setting out a dedicated regulatory framework for MVNO operations and their relationships with host network operators (HNOs). Under the evolving framework, host network operators are expected to give prospective MVNOs clear information on technical and commercial requirements upfront. The draft proposes tighter, clearly defined timelines for host operators to acknowledge MVNO hosting requests and confirm readiness to proceed. The draft further requires parties to set up a joint onboarding working group upon confirming readiness, and prohibits HNOs from unjustifiably or indefinitely delaying onboarding. The draft envisages a fixed outer limit for concluding commercial and technical agreements, in order to avoid indefinite delays. For investors, these constraints are designed to turn licence awards into live services on a predictable timetable, addressing a key execution risk in the MVNO business case. Commercial agreements will also sit under closer regulatory scrutiny. Executed MVNO commercial agreements are expected to be filed with the NCC within a defined period set by the regulator. Material amendments to MVNO agreements, including those related to pricing, numbering and interconnection, would be subject to NCC notification requirements. This level of visibility gives the regulator earlier sight of practices that could hinder competition or service quality. Governance, dispute resolution and consumer focus The draft Nigeria MVNO rules push governance deeper into contract design. Commercial agreements must clearly allocate responsibility for core operational obligations, including know-your-customer checks, activation approvals, subscriber complaint handling and compliance obligations for eSIM services. Existing MVNO–HNO contracts would need to be reviewed and updated to comply with the new framework within a transition period set by the NCC. Dispute management is formalised. Each commercial agreement must include an escalation ladder that separates technical from commercial issues and sets clear response times. The draft envisages a structured escalation ladder for technical and commercial disputes, with defined time limits for escalation to technical leads and then to executive level. If the parties still cannot resolve matters, either may refer the dispute to the NCC, and retaliatory measures such as service disruption are barred while the dispute is in progress. This structure aims to prevent the kind of protracted conflict that can derail MVNO launches and undermine network reliability. On the customer side, the rules seek to ensure that MVNO subscribers receive comparable treatment to host-network customers. HNOs may not unfairly limit or restrict MVNO traffic, a safeguard intended to support quality of service and non-discriminatory access. MVNOs must maintain transparent tariffs, accessible complaint channels and effective internal dispute resolution mechanisms, while carrying primary responsibility for subscriber relationships and customer care, despite their reliance on host infrastructure. They must also comply with the NCC’s wider consumer protection requirements. For investors, the direction of travel is clear. According to analysts, the NCC’s MVNO work aims to convert MVNOs from a regulatory concept into a functioning competitive layer that can extend coverage, sharpen pricing and increase service innovation. If the draft is finalised in its current form and enforced consistently, it could de-risk MVNO execution, improve visibility on contractual and regulatory exposure, and expand the pipeline of bankable digital-infrastructure and consumer-connectivity plays across Nigeria’s mass-market and underserved segments. title: Angola Oil Reform is Reshaping Investment in Africa’s Energy Sector
summary:
Angola oil reform is reshaping capital flows across Africa. See how Luanda's institutional overhaul is attracting investors.

The post Angola Oil Reform is Reshaping Investment in Africa’s Energy Sector appeared first on FurtherAfrica.
full_text: Angola Oil Reform is Reshaping Investment in Africa’s Energy Sector Angola oil reform is reshaping capital flows across Africa. See how Luanda's institutional overhaul is attracting investors. The post Angola Oil Reform is Reshaping Investment in Africa’s Energy Sector appeared first on FurtherAfrica. Angola oil reform has become the region’s clearest example of how decisive policy shifts can redirect capital flows in a mature hydrocarbon economy.   Angola’s oil sector is showing how fast policy can shift capital flows when governments move decisively on investor constraints. Angola oil reform is now shorthand in the region for separating regulation from operations, opening acreage on flexible terms and backing hydrocarbons with clear political support, even as the country starts to reposition gas and downstream assets for a more diversified energy system. From structural overhaul to flexible licensing In the new book Crude Oil: Power, Turnaround, and Transformation in Angola, African Energy Chamber Executive Chairman NJ Ayuk argues that Angola has shifted from near-decline to stabilisation through a deliberate mix of institutional reform and commercial flexibility. Under President João Manuel Gonçalves Lourenço and Mineral Resources, Oil and Gas Minister Diamantino Pedro Azevedo, Luanda moved early to tackle two core weaknesses: thin exploration activity and opaque governance. The government created the National Oil, Gas and Biofuels Agency (ANPG) as an independent upstream regulator and restructured Sonangol so it could focus on operations rather than licensing and policy. The ANPG took over concession management and launched a multi-year licensing strategy targeting 60 concessions, with 40 already awarded. This shift has given international oil companies a clearer counterpart on regulation, while allowing Sonangol to expand its operating portfolio, deepen partnerships and prepare for a potential initial public offering. Institutional change alone was not enough to reverse decline trends. To keep investment flowing through volatile price cycles, Angola introduced a Permanent Offer Regime in 2021. The scheme allows the state to promote and negotiate concessions outside traditional bid rounds, with blocks remaining continuously available for offers. Between 2021 and 2023, 27 blocks were awarded under this more flexible framework, signalling that capital is responsive when barriers to entry fall. The regime has also lowered the bar for smaller independents, which often cannot wait for infrequent, rigid licensing rounds. Angola then targeted the long tail of existing resources. A dedicated framework for marginal fields opened a path for smaller players to develop assets that larger operators had sidelined as sub-economic. In parallel, the Incremental Production Decree, launched in 2024, incentivises reinvestment in mature fields by improving the economics of incremental barrels. Ayuk notes that the decree could support recovery of up to 500 million additional barrels and extend field life by as much as 20 years. ExxonMobil has already made the first discovery under this regime at the Likember-01 well on Block 15, underlining that majors still see upside in Angola’s brownfield portfolio when fiscal and regulatory terms align. Gas, downstream and the push to capture more value The reform agenda extends beyond crude. Angola holds an estimated 11 trillion cubic feet of natural gas and is now positioning gas as a strategic pillar alongside oil. While the Angola LNG plant has exported associated gas since 2012, policy has shifted to support dedicated gas projects. A 2018 Gas Monetisation Law and a Gas Master Plan approved in 2025 provide a coherent framework for investors across the gas value chain. Since then, the New Gas Consortium has brought the country’s first non-associated gas project online in 2026, and Azule Energy has reported the first dedicated gas discovery in Block 1/14. This starts to pivot Angola from flaring-driven associated gas to a more sustainable gas portfolio that can underpin both exports and domestic demand. Downstream, Angola is trying to close a structural gap that has long eroded value. Despite producing more than one million barrels per day, the country still imports around 70% of its refined products. To shift that balance, the government created the petroleum products regulator, Instituto Regulador dos Derivados do Petróleo (IRDP), and set out plans for three new refineries to complement the existing Luanda plant. The Cabinda refinery has entered operation since 2025, while the Lobito project is seeking financing and Soyo remains in preparation. If delivered, these plants would reduce import dependence and keep more margins onshore, with knock-on benefits for foreign-exchange stability and industrial employment. For other African producers, the Angola oil reform story offers a practical template rather than an abstract policy wish list. The sequence matters: clarify institutions, liberalise access to acreage, then target marginal and mature resources, while in parallel building gas and downstream strategies that support fiscal resilience. As Angola’s upstream stabilises and new gas and refining assets move forward, investors will watch three signals in particular: the pace of remaining licence awards, final investment decisions on Lobito and Soyo, and how quickly the incremental production and marginal field regimes translate into sustained plateau output rather than a short-term bump. South Africa platform economy shifts from open markets to digital platforms — logistics depth defines the next winners.

full_text: Logistics Emerges as the Key Battleground in South Africa’s Platform Economy South Africa platform economy shifts from open markets to digital platforms — logistics depth defines the next winners. The post Logistics Emerges as the Key Battleground in South Africa’s Platform Economy appeared first on FurtherAfrica. The South Africa platform economy is shifting from open markets to tightly managed digital systems — and logistics capability is emerging as the defining source of competitive advantage.   Platforms as economic rails South Africa’s consumer economy is moving from open markets towards tightly managed digital platforms. The shift is reshaping how goods, services and labour are accessed. It is concentrating power in firms that control logistics as much as code. The South Africa platform economy is no longer just about convenience. It is about coordination. Platforms increasingly sit between consumers, suppliers and workers, and they manage the flow between them. Uber, Takealot and Mr D illustrate the model. They do not simply match buyers and sellers. They organise movement, fulfilment and access. Grocery delivery apps work in the same way. Their value comes from the systems behind the app. That matters because the strongest platforms are not always the best-known brands. They are often the ones with the deepest logistics reach. Routing, delivery density, inventory visibility and response times are now core sources of advantage. In practice, supply chains have become strategic infrastructure. This changes the structure of competition. Traditional markets were fragmented and visible. Platforms centralise that visibility inside a single digital layer. As a result, they shape which suppliers reach customers, which businesses gain scale, and which services remain accessible. The core point is clear. The platform economy is less about software alone, and more about supply chain capability. Labour and power are being mediated The South Africa platform economy also changes work. Drivers, delivery workers and service providers increasingly operate through algorithmic systems rather than conventional employers. That creates a new kind of dependence. Consumers depend on platforms for access and convenience. Businesses depend on them for reach. Workers depend on them for income. Restaurants, retailers and suppliers also operate inside ecosystems they do not fully control. This is especially important in South Africa. The country combines inequality, uneven infrastructure and patchy digital access. In such conditions, platforms often gain ground quickly because they offer predictability where public systems can be unreliable. However, the same features that make platforms useful also make them powerful. They can influence which firms stay visible. They can steer demand. They can define the terms of participation. For investors, that means the real opportunity is not limited to consumer-facing apps. The more durable winners may be the companies building private economic rails across transport, retail, food delivery and financial services. Those rails are shaped by logistics depth, data, fulfilment systems and operational control. The strategic question for the market is how far this model spreads. Investors should watch the platforms that deepen their logistics networks fastest, because they are most likely to define the next phase of the South Africa platform economy. full_text: Africa Advisory Growth: A&M Opens Cape Town Office Africa advisory growth accelerates as Alvarez & Marsal launches its first African office in Cape Town to serve global capital flows. The post Africa Advisory Growth: A&M Opens Cape Town Office appeared first on FurtherAfrica. A&M is targeting infrastructure, energy and stressed assets in Africa.   Alvarez & Marsal‘s push into Africa signals rising demand for execution-heavy restructuring and transaction support. That demand is growing faster than the supply of pan-regional advisory platforms able to deploy senior teams on the ground. A&M moves in as global funds scale Africa allocations Alvarez & Marsal (A&M) launched its first African office in Cape Town in May 2026. The office creates a launchpad for mandates across South Africa and the wider continent. A&M says the Cape Town office is aimed at helping organisations improve operational performance, strengthen resilience and deliver greater returns from existing infrastructure and capital-intensive assets. Its focus includes infrastructure, energy and capital-intensive industrial assets, including mining-related mandates. Global funds are seeking exposure to power, transport, digital infrastructure and critical minerals. These deals often involve complex capital structures and partnership models. As a result, investors increasingly need advisers that combine restructuring, transaction and performance-improvement skills — not pure strategy support. A&M’s integrated transaction advisory teams already work for private equity and sovereign wealth investors globally. Extending this model into Africa gives A&M a platform to follow global clients into the continent. It also allows the firm to compete for mandates against more established audit-linked advisers. Advisory gap widens as demand outpaces pan-African capacity The core investor story is a growing mismatch. Capital targeting Africa is scaling rapidly. Yet the pool of firms able to execute complex restructurings and transformations across borders remains small. Large infrastructure and energy transactions typically cut across multiple jurisdictions, currencies and regulatory regimes. They often involve state-owned enterprises or public-private partnerships. That raises the premium on advisers who can structure workouts, stabilise assets and drive operational change while managing political and stakeholder risk. A&M’s Cape Town hub is designed to serve both local corporates and international investors. The move also reflects wider interest in Africa’s advisory market as global firms reassess the continent’s risk-return profile. Energy transition, supply-chain diversification and the race for critical minerals are all reshaping that calculus. Execution-heavy advisers are likely to see steady deal flow not only from new investments, but also from legacy assets. Those assets require restructuring or operational repositioning to meet new standards on climate, governance and digital integration. For investors, A&M’s entry provides another signal that Africa’s deal and restructuring market is maturing. The advisory ecosystem is starting to catch up with capital flows. However, pan-African capacity remains thin relative to demand, especially outside South Africa and a few major hubs. That imbalance suggests continued opportunity for specialist firms, joint ventures and local partnerships that can scale advisory capability across the continent. For institutional investors and development finance institutions, the practical takeaway is clear. Early engagement with capable advisers will be critical to originate, structure and fix complex assets at speed. Investors should monitor how quickly firms like A&M can build out local capacity beyond South Africa and whether new entrants will deepen the advisory bench across the continent’s key growth corridors. Keypoints: Hundreds of residents protested against a proposed US Ebola quarantine facility in Nanyuki Kenya’s High Court has temporarily halted the project pending legal proceedings Local communities fear potential health risks despite government assurances HUNDREDS of residents in Kenya’s Nanyuki town protested on Monday against a proposed US-backed Ebola quarantine facility at a military base, escalating opposition to a project that has already been temporarily suspended by the High Court. The dispute centres on a planned 50-bed quarantine unit intended to accommodate American citizens who may have been exposed to Ebola but are not displaying symptoms. While Kenyan and US officials have presented the facility as part of wider emergency preparedness efforts, many residents argue that its location near civilian communities could expose them to unnecessary health risks. Court order puts project on hold The controversy intensified on Friday when Kenya’s High Court ordered a temporary suspension of the project after petitioners filed a lawsuit claiming that the facility could endanger public health. According to Reuters, the quarantine unit is planned for a Kenyan Air Force base in Laikipia County near Nanyuki. The facility was expected to become operational last week before the court intervened. Kenya’s Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale defended the initiative over the weekend, saying it formed part of broader efforts to strengthen national emergency response systems and improve preparedness for potential disease outbreaks. US officials said the facility would only host individuals who had been exposed to the virus but were not exhibiting symptoms, and that strict health and safety measures would be maintained at all times. Residents fear community exposure Despite those assurances, opposition within Nanyuki has continued to grow. Video footage obtained by Reuters showed protesters gathering near the planned site, blowing whistles, carrying placards and erecting makeshift barricades on roads leading towards the military installation. Smoke was seen rising from burning debris placed on parts of the roadway. Local residents estimated that several hundred people participated in the demonstrations. Television footage broadcast by Kenya’s NTV and Citizen TV showed groups of protesters assembled outside the air base, where soldiers and military vehicles were stationed. Patrick Wahome, one of the protest organisers, said residents remained concerned about the possibility of disease transmission within the community. ‘Nanyuki is a very small town. Military personnel who serve at the base live among us, and our children attend the same schools,’ Wahome said. ‘If anything goes wrong, the entire community could be affected. We are demonstrating because we believe our lives and health are at stake.’ Organisers have reportedly called for the permanent cancellation of the project. Increased military activity raises questions The proposed facility has also attracted attention because of increased military activity in the area. A Reuters witness reported a heightened security presence around roads leading to the base over the weekend, with additional police and military personnel deployed near the installation. Flight-tracking data reviewed by Reuters indicated that a US military C-130 transport aircraft landed in Nanyuki on Friday. Residents also reported seeing aircraft flying towards the base over the weekend, although Reuters could not independently confirm whether they belonged to the United States military. Diplomats and security analysts said the movements appeared consistent with preparations linked to the quarantine facility despite the court’s suspension order. Neither US military officials nor Kenyan authorities publicly commented on the reported flights. US-Kenya partnership under scrutiny The controversy has also drawn attention to the broader security and defence relationship between Kenya and the United States. Kenya is one of Washington’s closest strategic partners in East Africa and hosts regular military cooperation programmes, joint exercises and counterterrorism initiatives. The planned quarantine facility appears to be linked to emergency contingency planning for US personnel in the region, although officials have released limited public information about its long-term role or operational arrangements. The lack of detailed public consultation has become a major source of concern among residents and civil society groups questioning the project’s location and oversight. The dispute follows growing public scrutiny after the court-ordered suspension of the US-backed Ebola facility, intensifying debate over transparency and community safety. Ebola concerns remain politically sensitive The debate comes at a time when African governments continue to strengthen surveillance and emergency response systems against infectious diseases. Although Kenya has not experienced a major Ebola outbreak, the country has previously increased border screening and preparedness measures during outbreaks elsewhere on the continent. Public health authorities remain alert to the risk of imported cases during regional health emergencies. Health experts generally regard quarantine facilities as important tools for preventing disease transmission during outbreaks. However, community acceptance often becomes a critical factor in determining whether such facilities can operate successfully. The dispute in Nanyuki highlights the challenge governments face when balancing public health preparedness with local concerns about safety, transparency and public trust. Businesses feel impact of protests The demonstrations also disrupted economic activity in the town. Patrick Maina, who owns a local café, said uncertainty surrounding the facility and the protests had affected business operations. ‘We have not opened since morning, and there is concern the situation could become worse if tensions continue,’ he told Reuters. Nanyuki serves as an important commercial and tourism hub in central Kenya, and business owners fear prolonged unrest could affect visitor numbers and local trade. Future of facility remains uncertain For now, the future of the quarantine unit remains unclear as legal proceedings continue. The High Court’s temporary suspension means the project cannot proceed until judges review arguments presented by both supporters and opponents of the plan. The outcome could have broader implications for how Kenya manages future public health infrastructure projects involving international partners, particularly when local communities raise concerns over transparency, safety and consultation. As the legal battle unfolds, the dispute is increasingly becoming a test of how governments balance public health preparedness, national security cooperation and community concerns in an era of heightened awareness about infectious disease risks.The post Kenya protests US Ebola quarantine facility first appeared on Africa Briefing.

title: Britain avoids £100m Rwanda asylum payout
summary:
Keypoints: Court rejects Rwanda’s claim for additional payments Britain avoids a potential £100m liability Labour says taxpayers are protected from further costs BRITAIN will not have to pay Rwanda an additional £100m after an international arbitration panel ruled in favour of London, according to a Reuters report, ending a dispute over the cancelled Rwanda asylum […]

Keypoints: Court rejects Rwanda’s claim for additional payments Britain avoids a potential £100m liability Labour says taxpayers are protected from further costs BRITAIN will not have to pay Rwanda an additional £100m after an international arbitration panel ruled in favour of London, according to a Reuters report, ending a dispute over the cancelled Rwanda asylum agreement. The decision closes one of the final unresolved issues arising from the abandoned UK-Rwanda migration partnership, a flagship Conservative policy that was scrapped by Prime Minister Keir Starmer after Labour’s election victory. The ruling removes a potential £100m liability for British taxpayers and brings to an end a contentious legal dispute between London and Kigali. Court rejects Rwanda compensation claim The asylum arrangement was introduced by the Conservative government in 2022 as part of efforts to reduce irregular migration across the English Channel. Under the policy, asylum seekers arriving in Britain without authorisation could be relocated to Rwanda, where their asylum applications would be processed. Individuals granted protection would remain in Rwanda rather than return to the UK. The programme quickly became one of the most controversial immigration policies in modern British politics. Legal challenges, human rights concerns and political opposition repeatedly delayed implementation. Britain’s Supreme Court ruled in 2023 that Rwanda could not be considered a safe destination for asylum seekers under the framework then in place. The decision forced the government to negotiate a revised treaty and introduce emergency legislation aimed at reviving the scheme. As previously reported in the UK Court of Appeal ruling against the Rwanda deportation plan, the policy had already faced significant legal setbacks before eventually reaching the UK’s highest court. Labour scrapped the scheme The Rwanda plan was abandoned shortly after Labour won the 2024 general election. Starmer described the policy as ineffective and argued it had failed to deter migrants from attempting dangerous Channel crossings. His government pledged instead to focus resources on tackling people-smuggling gangs and strengthening border enforcement. Earlier reporting on Labour’s decision to scrap the £10bn Rwanda asylum scheme detailed criticism of the programme’s cost and limited practical results. Labour ministers said the arbitration ruling vindicated their decision to terminate the scheme and demonstrated that taxpayers should not be required to fund additional payments linked to a policy that never became operational. Following the cancellation, Rwanda maintained that Britain remained bound by certain financial obligations contained within the agreement and subsequently launched arbitration proceedings. Rwanda sought £100m in payments At the centre of the dispute were two scheduled payments worth £50m each that Rwanda argued it was entitled to receive despite the programme’s termination. Kigali said it had invested considerable resources preparing accommodation facilities, administrative systems and support services for migrants expected to arrive under the arrangement. The arbitration panel, however, found that exchanges between British and Rwandan officials after the policy was cancelled effectively demonstrated a shared understanding that the payments would no longer be due. The ruling also dismissed claims that Britain had breached other elements of the agreement. Arbitrators concluded that diplomatic communications exchanged after Labour cancelled the policy showed both governments understood the outstanding payments would not proceed. The panel found no legal basis for Rwanda’s argument that Britain remained obligated to make the final instalments after the agreement had effectively been terminated. Earlier this year, Rwanda’s arbitration case against Britain over the axed migrant deal highlighted Kigali’s push for compensation. A separate report on the UK-Rwanda dispute over unpaid £50m instalments examined growing tensions over the agreement’s termination clauses. Expensive policy never fully launched Despite years of political debate and legal preparation, no asylum seekers were forcibly deported to Rwanda under the scheme. The policy nevertheless generated substantial costs for British taxpayers. Hundreds of millions of pounds were spent on payments to Rwanda, legal proceedings, detention facilities and operational planning before Labour cancelled the programme. Critics argued the initiative consumed large sums of public money without delivering meaningful reductions in migrant arrivals, while supporters maintained it represented a necessary deterrent against illegal crossings. Political implications remain The ruling is expected to strengthen Labour’s argument that cancelling the scheme was the correct financial and policy decision. Government officials welcomed the outcome, saying taxpayers would not face further costs linked to a programme that never became fully operational. Rwanda has consistently maintained that it acted in good faith throughout the partnership and fulfilled its obligations under the agreement. Before Labour formally ended the policy, Rwanda had already been informed of Britain’s intention to terminate the deportation agreement. Despite the dispute, Britain and Rwanda continue to maintain broader diplomatic engagement through trade, investment, development cooperation and regional security initiatives, limiting the wider impact of the arbitration case on bilateral relations. While the arbitration decision settles the financial dispute, migration remains one of the most politically sensitive issues in Britain. Pressure continues to mount on the government to reduce small-boat crossings, and immigration is expected to remain a major issue ahead of future elections. The ruling may therefore close the legal chapter of the Rwanda scheme, but the broader debate over Britain’s asylum and border policies is far from over.  The post Britain avoids £100m Rwanda asylum payout first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Inquiry hears allegations of corruption and organised crime infiltration Witnesses testify about missing cocaine seizures and procurement irregularities Final report expected in August following the last phase of hearings SOUTH Africa’s anti-corruption inquiry has completed its second phase after hearing allegations of police misconduct, organised crime infiltration and failures in the handling of major cocaine seizures. The Madlanga Commission’s final report is expected in August. The commission was established after KwaZulu-Natal Police Commissioner Gen Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi alleged in 2025 that criminal syndicates had infiltrated sections of South Africa’s police service and government. As the inquiry enters its final phase, its findings could have far-reaching implications for policing, governance and anti-corruption efforts across the country. The allegations triggered national attention and led President Cyril Ramaphosa to establish the commission to examine claims of corruption, criminal infiltration and misconduct within South Africa’s security institutions. The commission, chaired by retired Constitutional Court Justice Mbuyiseli Madlanga, submitted its second interim report to President Cyril Ramaphosa on Friday. Although the report has not been made public, testimony presented during the latest hearings has revealed allegations involving senior police officials, suspected organised crime figures and controversial law enforcement operations. Procurement contract under scrutiny One of the most closely watched testimonies came from Brig Rachel Matjeng, who oversaw a police healthcare services tender awarded in 2024 to Medicare24 Tshwane District, a company linked to businessman Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala. The contract was terminated a year later and several senior police officials, including Matjeng, have since been charged in connection with the procurement process. None has entered a plea in court. The case reflects broader concerns around alleged corruption within South Africa’s security institutions, including Africa Briefing’s report on graft charges against South Africa’s police chief. Appearing before the commission, Matjeng denied receiving bribes from Matlala. Instead, she described their relationship as personal and said he had provided gifts during the course of their association. She rejected social media allegations that she had received cosmetic surgery as a benefit, telling commissioners that Matlala had only assisted her in obtaining supplies of the diabetes and weight-loss medication Ozempic. Matlala has not yet appeared before the commission. Missing cocaine raises questions Another major focus of the hearings centred on the handling of two significant cocaine seizures in 2021. The first involved 541kg of cocaine intercepted in Durban and valued at more than 200m rand ($12.2m). Months after the seizure, the drugs were stolen from a Hawks facility in what investigators suspect may have been an inside operation. Maj-Gen Hendrik Flynn of the Hawks told the commission that numerous procedural failures contributed to the theft. These included inadequate crime-scene processing, failure to gather forensic evidence and the decision to store the narcotics at a facility with insufficient security measures. Questions were also raised about a separate 700kg cocaine seizure in Johannesburg in July 2021. Lt Col Nkoana Sebola testified that circumstances surrounding the operation were suspicious, particularly because officials involved allegedly operated outside their authorised jurisdictions. Commission hearings revealed that officers entered premises without a search warrant and removed suspected narcotics before specialist investigators arrived. One official, analytics officer Marumo Magane, acknowledged several mistakes in handling evidence. He admitted to actions including loading confiscated drugs into his police vehicle and interfering with exhibits. Justice Madlanga criticised Magane’s conduct, suggesting he lacked the expertise required for such an operation. Magane agreed with the assessment during his testimony. Although several individuals were arrested following the incident, prosecutors later dropped charges citing insufficient prospects for a successful prosecution. The inquiry also heard that 136kg of cocaine later disappeared from secure storage at a forensic laboratory. The allegations have intensified scrutiny of police oversight systems. Parliament has previously raised concerns about accountability failures within the service, including issues highlighted in Africa Briefing’s report on the SAPS ghost worker investigation. Political fixer faces legal troubles Businessman and political figure Oupa ‘Brown’ Mogotsi also returned to the spotlight during the hearings. Mogotsi has repeatedly denied allegations that he played a role in facilitating corruption within police structures. Last year he told the commission he had survived an assassination attempt after gunfire struck his vehicle east of Johannesburg. His appearance before the commission was marked by controversy after he made claims against senior public figures that he later withdrew. When he returned for cross-examination in May, Mogotsi challenged the impartiality of the commission’s evidence leader and refused to answer several questions, citing concerns about self-incrimination. Shortly after his testimony, Mogotsi was arrested by a specialist police task team established to investigate evidence emerging from the commission. He now faces charges linked to allegations that the reported attempt on his life was staged. Mogotsi denies the accusations and is seeking bail. Organised crime allegations remain central Central to the inquiry are allegations that organised crime networks may have cultivated influence within sections of law enforcement and government institutions. Matlala was previously named during testimony as an alleged figure within a criminal network accused of involvement in drug trafficking, kidnappings, contract killings and vehicle hijackings. He remains in custody facing multiple criminal charges, including attempted murder, all of which he denies. The broader concerns raised before the commission echo wider debates about accountability, governance and corruption that have affected South Africa’s political landscape in recent years, including developments covered in Africa Briefing’s reporting on corruption-related pressure facing Ramaphosa’s administration. The allegations have also renewed attention on the challenges facing law enforcement agencies as they confront increasingly sophisticated criminal networks operating across Southern Africa. Final phase approaches The commission’s final phase is scheduled to begin next month and is expected to include testimony from additional key figures, including Matlala. The inquiry arrives at a critical moment for South Africa’s institutions, with public confidence in policing and governance under renewed scrutiny. Analysts say the commission’s final findings could shape future reforms within the police service and influence broader anti-corruption initiatives. South Africans are now awaiting the commission’s final report, due in August, which is expected to be made public and could have significant implications for the country’s law enforcement agencies and broader anti-corruption efforts. The commission’s work has become a major test of South Africa’s efforts to rebuild public confidence in state institutions following years of corruption scandals and allegations of state capture. Whether its findings ultimately lead to prosecutions, reforms or both will be closely watched by citizens, political leaders and law enforcement agencies alike.The post South Africa inquiry exposes police corruption claims first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Mahama backs constitutional reforms to allow dual citizens to become MPs and ministers Ato Forson says Ghana has recovered from the economic crisis inherited in 2025 Diaspora members demand greater political inclusion, accountability and investment opportunities PRESIDENT John Dramani Mahama has announced plans to amend Ghana’s Constitution to allow dual citizens living abroad to serve as members of parliament and ministers, telling a town hall meeting in north London that overseas Ghanaians deserve a greater role in shaping the country’s future. The proposal was one of several major announcements made during a diaspora town hall in Wood Green on May 31, where Mahama, Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson and other senior government officials sought to reassure overseas Ghanaians that Ghana’s economy had stabilised, investor confidence was returning and the diaspora would play a larger role in national development. The reforms form part of a broader constitutional review process currently being prepared for parliamentary consideration. The event, held on the eve of the Ghana-UK Investment Summit scheduled for June 1, brought together members of the Ghanaian community in the United Kingdom, government officials and business leaders. Mahama returned to office following the December 2024 elections and has made economic recovery, constitutional reform and the proposed 24-hour economy programme central pillars of his administration. Diaspora reforms proposed Mahama described overseas Ghanaians as Ghana’s ’17th region’, arguing that their contribution to the country’s development justifies a stronger voice in governance. ‘We have 16 physical regions in Ghana, but we have one virtual region which is our diaspora abroad,’ he said. ‘Your remittances have reached the highest ever above $7bn — $7.8bn actually last year. I dare say that probably that is much larger than many regions are contributing to the GDP in Ghana.’ The president said the constitutional review process would seek to remove restrictions preventing many dual citizens from participating fully in public life. ‘We currently have legislation before Parliament to review the 1992 Constitution to allow Ghanaians in the diaspora who hold other passports or dual passports to be able to participate in our politics at parliamentary and ministerial level,’ Mahama said. Economy ‘back on track’ Earlier, Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson told the gathering that Ghana had emerged from one of the most severe economic crises in its modern history. ‘President Mahama inherited a terrible economy, an economy in difficult times,’ Forson said. ‘Ghana went through a very difficult economic crisis in a lifetime. I do not recall that our country had ever gone through such level of economic crisis. The scale of the crisis was profound.’ The minister cited currency instability, high inflation, loss of investor confidence and Ghana’s exclusion from international capital markets as some of the challenges facing the country when the administration assumed office. He said recent indicators showed significant improvement. ‘The good news is that today our country is back. We are back,’ Forson declared. Forson said Ghana recorded six percent GDP growth in 2025 and 7.6 percent non-oil GDP growth, while inflation, debt sustainability indicators and borrowing costs had improved substantially. ‘All of this points to one important thing. These results affirm that fiscal prudence and discipline always deliver results,’ he said. The finance minister ended with a direct appeal to overseas Ghanaians. ‘Ghana is open for business. We welcome you. Come home and contribute.’ Mahama touts recovery and industrialisation Mahama argued that difficult economic decisions taken during the first months of his administration had restored confidence and stabilised key indicators. ‘The sacrifices that Ghanaians made have paid off and Ghana is back again. Ghana is working again,’ he said. He claimed Ghana’s recovery had attracted international attention. ‘Ghana has become the poster boy for economic recovery across the world. Anytime they go for the spring meetings of the World Bank and the IMF, everybody is pointing to Ghana and saying, ‘Go to Ghana and learn how they did it,’ Mahama said. The president also highlighted plans to increase local value addition in strategic sectors. ‘We are about to start to refine our own crude,’ Mahama announced, revealing that Ghanaian crude oil would soon be processed domestically through the Tema Oil Refinery rather than exported entirely in raw form. He disclosed that agreements had been signed for approximately $2bn in new investment in the Jubilee oil fields and a further $1.5bn investment in the OCTP field operated by ENI, aimed at increasing oil and gas production while strengthening Ghana’s energy security. Mahama also said the government had rebuilt a $500m World Bank guarantee supporting gas supplies and had significantly reduced debts owed to independent power producers, helping to stabilise the energy sector. He added that similar value-addition efforts were under way in the cocoa sector, where the government wants to increase local processing and export more finished products across Africa under the African Continental Free Trade Area. The president said the reforms complemented broader efforts to overhaul Ghana’s extractive industries through measures designed to improve transparency, increase local participation and strengthen state revenues from natural resources. Recent changes have included new mining sector reforms aimed at reshaping the country’s resource governance framework. Accountability drive gathers pace Governance and accountability featured prominently in Mahama’s remarks. The president disclosed that approximately 36 investigations were active and said public officials who abused their offices would face consequences regardless of political affiliation. ‘We’re not interested in witch-hunting anybody. We’re interested in accountability,’ Mahama said. He also outlined plans to use blockchain technology, artificial intelligence and specialised audit courts to strengthen financial oversight. ‘Friends to all, enemies to none’ Touching on foreign policy, Mahama said Ghana would continue pursuing constructive relations with countries across competing geopolitical blocs. ‘We are friends to all, enemies to none,’ he said, listing partners including the United Kingdom, United States, France, Germany, Russia, Ukraine, Iran and Israel. The president said Ghana’s priority was promoting peace and international cooperation at a time of growing global instability. Diaspora presses for greater inclusion The question-and-answer session reflected growing demands among overseas Ghanaians for a stronger role in national development. A representative of the East London branch of the ruling NDC noted that the diaspora contributes almost $8bn annually to Ghana’s economy and questioned why overseas citizens still felt excluded from key decision-making despite being recognised as the country’s ’17th region’. He also asked how proposals linked to the government’s 24-hour economy initiative could be submitted directly to policymakers after previous submissions appeared to disappear within official channels. Responding, Mahama said constitutional reforms were specifically intended to remove barriers that had prevented many overseas Ghanaians from participating fully in national life. ‘Being the 17th region, you must be free to be able to come home and participate,’ he said, adding that several members of his administration had previously been active members of diaspora organisations in the UK. Another participant called for all public institutions to publish annual audited accounts to strengthen transparency and accountability and avoid recurring controversies over public finances. Mahama responded by revealing that some state-owned enterprises had failed to submit audited accounts for as long as seven years before his administration intensified oversight. ‘We’ve made it part of their key performance indicators,’ he said. ‘If you have not presented your audited accounts, you haven’t presented your annual reports, the road is your face, you go home.’ He added that several state-owned enterprises had already moved from loss-making to profit-making positions following reforms and stricter accountability measures. A further question focused on creating a national database that would connect skilled diaspora professionals with opportunities in Ghana and help transform ‘brain drain’ into ‘brain gain’. Mahama acknowledged the concern but cautioned against rushed relocation decisions. ‘There’s brain drain and there’s brain gain,’ he said. ‘Take your time, look for what you want to do when you get back. You can even start it and make sure that it is grounded before you relocate.’ The president argued that migration was a natural part of human history and that Ghana should focus on ensuring that citizens abroad remained connected to national development regardless of where they lived. Questions were also raised about arrangements for Ghanaians abroad hoping to attend the Black Stars’ matches at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Mahama said the government would not fund travel and accommodation because of the high cost involved, estimating that supporting a single fan could cost around $11,000. ‘If you want to attend the game, you will get a ticket to attend the game,’ he said, adding that Ghanaian communities in Canada, Boston and Philadelphia were already being organised to support the national team. The London town hall formed part of Mahama’s wider UK programme in the United Kingdom. The visit also includes meetings with British officials, discussions with investors, an engagement at Chatham House and other high-level events aimed at attracting new capital and deepening economic ties between Ghana and the United Kingdom. The government is also seeking to reassure investors that Ghana can maintain fiscal discipline and macroeconomic stability following its exit from the IMF-supported programme in May, as it looks to consolidate recent economic gains and strengthen investor confidence.The post Mahama moves to allow diaspora MPs first appeared on Africa Briefing.
